# Schooling the First Children: The Obamas Weigh a Timeless Presidential Decision

As President-elect Barack Obama and Michelle Obama prepare for their move to Washington, they face a decision that has confronted first families for generations: where to educate their children within the fishbowl of White House life. For daughters Malia, 10, and Sasha, 7, the choice carries implications far beyond the classroom, touching on questions of privacy, security, and the delicate balance between a normal childhood and life in the national spotlight.

## The Weight of Precedent

The schooling of presidential children has long reflected both the personalities of first families and the political currents of their eras. Perhaps no comparison looms larger than that of the Kennedys, whose young children captivated a nation in the early 1960s.

Jacqueline Kennedy famously established a small school right inside the White House for her daughter Caroline and a handful of children from families in the Kennedy circle. The arrangement allowed the first lady an unusual degree of control over her children's early education and privacy—a solution born of both Mrs. Kennedy's strong views on child-rearing and the intense public fascination with the young family.

## The Public School Choice

Not every first family opted for private arrangements. When Jimmy Carter arrived in Washington in 1977, he made a deliberate and symbolically potent choice: his daughter Amy attended Thaddeus Stevens Elementary, a public school in the District of Columbia. For a president who cultivated an image of populist authenticity and walked the inaugural parade route on foot, enrolling Amy in public school reinforced the message of a family in touch with ordinary Americans.

The decision was not without complications. Amy Carter's presence brought Secret Service agents into the public school environment, and the young girl became an object of media attention that occasionally intruded on her education.

## The Clinton Approach

Two decades later, the Clintons charted a different course. When Bill Clinton took office in 1993, he and Hillary Clinton enrolled their daughter Chelsea, then 12, at Sidwell Friends, the prestigious private Quaker school in Washington. The Clintons cited privacy and security concerns, seeking to shield their only child from the relentless scrutiny that comes with adolescence in the White House.

The choice drew some criticism from public education advocates who wished the first family had made a more visible commitment to public schools. But the Clintons largely succeeded in giving Chelsea a measure of insulation during her teenage years, and Sidwell's experience handling high-profile families offered practical advantages.

## The Obamas' Considerations

For the Obamas, the calculus involves familiar factors weighed anew. In Chicago, Malia and Sasha attended the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools, a private institution—suggesting the family may be inclined toward a similar setting in Washington.

Security experts note that private schools, accustomed to enrolling children of diplomats, senators, and other prominent figures, are often better equipped to integrate the extraordinary Secret Service presence that follows first children. The daily logistics of protection—managing entrances, coordinating with staff, minimizing disruption—can be more seamlessly handled at institutions with prior experience.

Yet the symbolic pull of public education remains, particularly for a president whose campaign emphasized shared opportunity and civic connection. Whatever the Obamas decide, they will be navigating the same fundamental tension their predecessors faced: how to give their daughters something approaching a normal childhood while living at the most-watched address in America.

## A Personal Decision, A Public Interest

The schooling of the Obama daughters ultimately remains a family decision, one the president-elect and Mrs. Obama have signaled they intend to make on the basis of their children's needs. History suggests there is no single right answer—Kennedy, Carter, and Clinton each found different solutions suited to their moment and their family.

For Malia and Sasha, the coming years promise an experience unlike that of nearly any other American child. The school they attend will be their daily refuge from the extraordinary circumstances of their new life—and, if the Obamas follow the example of first families before them, a place where they can simply be children.
